paper_title: Venus-DefakerOne2: A Vision-Forensics Foundation Model with Broader Coverage

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-world forgery is inherently heterogeneous: it manifests not only as digital manipulation but also as physical spoofing, and is carried not only by images but also by videos. Despite substantial progress, a unified anti-forgery foundation model covering such a broad threat spectrum remains absent. In this paper, we present Venus-DefakerOne2, which substantially extends the forensic capability boundary along both the forgery-form and media-type dimensions. Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, it incorporates two key designs. Tide-Style-Tuning alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning to balance computational efficiency, generalization, and hard-sample fitting while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy. Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves new state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including DeepFake faces (96.7%), AI-generated images (93.3%), tampered documents (87.6%), manipulated natural images (89.6%), physical spoofs (93.1%), and AI-generated videos (96.0%). It significantly outperforms both specialized expert models and its predecessor, DefakerOne, establishing itself as a powerful and versatile foundation model for binary-decision forensic tasks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Visual media including images and videos has become the predominant carrier of information in the digital era Xiao et al. (2018); Xin et al. (2026), underpinning applications from news dissemination, social communication to identity authentication and judicial evidence Jiang et al. (2026c, 2025). Meanwhile, the proliferation of sophisticated acquisition devices, accessible editing tools, and generative AI models has dramatically lowered the barrier to fabricating and tampering with visual content. Forged media can bypass biometric verification Yuan et al. (2024a); Yu et al. (2024), deceive content moderation systems Gushchin et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025b), and manipulate public opinion at scale Ma et al. (2023); Hopf et al. (2026), posing substantial risks to information security and social trust. Consequently, detecting visual media forgery has emerged as fundamental problem that demands scalable and generalizable solutions. The landscape of real-world forgery, however, is far more heterogeneous than what most existing solutions assume (Ji-Zhe phenomenon Du et al. (2026a)). Along the forgery-form dimension, forgery is not limited to digital manipulation performed in the pixel or latent space (e.g., splicing, inpainting, and AI-generated imagery) Qu et al. (2026b); Wong et al. (2025); it also takes physical forms such as mask presentation attacks and document recapture attacks Tapia et al. (2026); Polevoy et al. (2022). Along the media-type dimension, forged content is carried not only by still images but also by videos, whose artifacts may reside in spatial textures, temporal dynamics, or cross-frame context. practical vision anti-forgery system must therefore cope with the full matrix of {digital, physical} {image, video}. Existing research, however, remains highly fragmented. The majority of detectors are designed for single scenario, such as specific manipulation type Park et al. (2023), fixed media format Hopf and Timofte (2025), or narrow acquisition setting Liu et al. (2022a), and generalize poorly beyond their training distribution. Worse still, different forgery forms have traditionally been studied in largely separate communities: digital image forensics Guo et al. (2026), face anti-spoofing Zhang et al. (2020a), document fraud detection Zeng et al. (2026), and video forensics Chen et al. (2026) each maintain their own benchmarks, assumptions, and model designs, even though the underlying goal, distinguishing genuine media from forged ones, is the same. This fragmentation prevents knowledge from being shared across scenarios and makes it costly to deploy and maintain separate model for every new threat Qu et al. (2024b). Our preliminary work, Venus-DeFakerOne Team (2026), took step toward unification by consolidating multi-scenario digital image forgery detection into single foundation model. Nevertheless, its capability boundary stops at digitally forged images: physical forgeries and video media lie entirely outside its scope. To the best of our knowledge, unified foundation model that simultaneously covers digital and physical forgery across both images and videos of multiple content types is still lacking. To build such comprehensive vision-forensics foundation model, we train Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) on large corpus of about 50M anti-forgery training data. Our training data are mainly sourced from three parts: public datasets, self-constructed datasets and manuallyannotated online-attack samples, covering the full matrix of {digital, physical} {image, video}. Despite the high diversity, training such model faces two key challenges, training cost and uneven data difficulty. This large-scale training corpus entails prohibitive computational cost under naive full-parameter training. Moreover, samples vary drastically in learning difficulty: some exhibit conspicuous artifacts that are fitted within few steps, while others contain only faint, elusive traces. static training regime either wastes capacity on trivially easy samples or suffers catastrophic forgetting of the base models general priors. 4 Additionally, there exists modality dilemma in video forensics. Forgery artifacts in videos distribute unevenly across dimensions. For some forgeries, evidence concentrates in temporal information and cross-frame contextflickering, motion inconsistency, and disrupted inter-frame continuity making the native video modality the natural choice. For others, evidence concentrates in the textural details of individual frames; feeding such clip as video brings little temporal gain and instead dilutes the models attention on spatial artifacts with redundant temporal tokens. Since which modality carries the stronger evidence is sample-dependent and unknown priori, one-size-fits-all input modality is inherently suboptimal. To address the training challenge, we propose Tide-Style Tuning, which reconciles computational efficiency, generalization, and fitting capacity. The training proceeds in three alternating phases, ebbing and flowing like tide. It begins with Adaptation Ebb, where we adopt the general-purpose pretrained Qwen3.5 model through LoRA-based fine-tuning. This step operates as warm-up, leveraging the strong priors of the Qwen3.5 backbone to promote generalization while mitigating catastrophic forgetting at low cost. The LoRA weights are then merged into the backbone, and the model undergoes full-parameter fine-tuning, unleashing the entire parameter budget to fit the large-scale diverse forgery corpus. Finally, training reverts to LoRA, which acts as regularizer that steers the model toward hard samples and prevents overfitting to the abundant easy ones. To solve the modality dilemma, we propose Modality Synergism, which aligns the two modalities on both the optimization side and the inference side. On the optimization side, our joint modality training presents each video to the model in both modalities simultaneouslythe native clip and the frame sequence extracted from it with an adaptive frame-rate strategyand optimizes an independent detection loss for each modality, forcing the shared backbone to internalize both spatial and temporal forensic evidence. On the inference side, our entropy-based test adaptation obtains predictions from both modalities, measures the certainty of each prediction by its Shannon entropy, and adopts the prediction of the more certain modality as the final decision. In this way, the model adaptively routes each sample, without any additional training or learned routing module, to the modality whose evidence is most salient for that sample. Through our proposed methods, our model, named Venus-DefakerOne2, effectively learns shared fundamental features of vision forgery across all common contents, forgery forms and media types. Fake videos in public video forensics dataset are generated by old generators released more than one year ago. To keep up the rapid development of AIGC video generation techniques, we constructed new video forensics benchmark, which termed as Realistic Rumor Video Benchmark (RRVBench). The fake videos in our RRVBench were generated by 7 latest closed-source video generators such as SeeDance 2.5 as well as 4 latest open-source video generators such as Minimax-H3. The video contents in our RRVBench focuses real-world rumor scenarios and minimizes the application gap. Our DefakerOne2 is evaluated on 53 visual media forgery detection benchmarks and 14 forgery localization benchmarks. With single set of 2B parameters, it ranks first on every one of the eight domains, achieving SOTA on 40/53 and 11/14 benchmarks, raising the average from 80.4 to 90.9 on images and from 57.6 to 95.7 on videos over its predecessor DefakerOne. The progress is qualitative: physical forgery, entirely outside the scope of DeFakerOne, climbs from 50.7 to 87.2, and on RRVBench DefakerOne2 reaches 95.3 while even 7B-parameter video-forensics MLLMs degenerate to near-chance guessing (best 69.8). Crucially, it is never outperformed by domain specialist on that specialists own domain, and its narrow cross-domain spread shows no domain pays for this generality. DefakerOne2 thus collapses fragmented assembly of scenario-specific detectors into one deployable foundation model. Figure 3 The overall framework of our DefakerOne2.

sections.content: 2.1 Model Architecture Overall Framework. Figure 3 illustrates the overall framework of DefakerOne2. Built upon multimodal large language model (MLLM), DefakerOne2 further introduces an Anomaly Magnifier module as an auxiliary encoder to strengthen the perception of fine-grained forensic cues, enabling single unified model to produce both image/video-level detection predictions and pixel-level localization masks. Specifically, the MLLM first perceives the input and performs global-level detection: guided by fixed prompt template tailored for efficient forensics, it analyzes the input, renders binary authenticity judgment, and generates corresponding confidence score for the downstream fine-grained segmentation task. The segmentation module then exploits this global forensic prior to conduct pixel-level analysis, yielding mask that highlights the tampered regions. Forgery Detection. DefakerOne2 adopts Qwen3.5-2B as its MLLM backbone. Since Qwen3.5-2B is native multimodal model, it can better leverage its world knowledge to implicitly reason about potential semantic anomalies, providing complementary high-level evidence for forgery analysis. In addition, the strong video understanding capability of Qwen3.5 makes it well suited to our unified image/video formulation. For detection, we query the MLLM with fixed and direct template for image/video-level binary classification. Our template query, Is this image/video real or fake? Answer only Real or Fake., guides the model to commit to its final conclusion in single output token, which maximizes both inference efficiency and the stability of the obtaining reliable prediction confidence. Forgery Localization. MLLMs are adept at global-level reasoning but often fall short in pixel-level analysis and prediction. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Anomaly Magnifier (AM) module as an auxiliary encoder. This encoder adopts the DINOMAC Qu et al. (2026a) backbone, which is DINOv3-Large Siméoni et al. (2025) architecture fine-tuned with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) adapter and forensic training strategies. Features from the MLLM vision encoder and the AM module are fed into mask decoder consisting of several convolutional layers for the final mask prediction. Inspired by APSC-Net Qu et al. Fine-tuning the model directly on our 50M corpus is highly non-trivial, as the data exhibit extreme diversity and long-tailed difficulty distribution. On the one hand, learning difficulty varies drastically across samples: some forgeries leave conspicuous artifacts that are fitted within few optimization steps, whereas others expose only faint, elusive traces that cannot be mastered within single training pass. On the other hand, data abundance varies drastically across subsets: some subsets share strong common patterns and appear in large volumes, while others are highly distinctive yet scarce. These disparities render any static training regime inadequate. single epoch is sufficient for the easy portion of the data but leaves the hard portion under-trained; simply scaling up the training budget not only incurs prohibitive cost but also increases the risk of overfitting to the easy majority. The choice of fine-tuning parameterization further sharpens the dilemma. Under full-parameter fine-tuning, the easy samples encountered at the beginning of training drive the model to rapidly overfit to dataset-specific cues and catastrophically forget its pretrained knowledge, while hard samples yield large gradients that erode the same knowledge and degrade generalization. Under LoRA fine-tuning, by contrast, the restricted parameter budget leaves the model unable to adequately fit tens of millions of diverse samples. This dilemma is compounded in practice: an anti-forgery foundation model must continually adapt to newly collected training data, and such continual adaptation inherits the same cost and overfitting risks. Overview. To mitigate this dilemma, we propose Tide-Style Tuning, which reconciles computational efficiency, generalization, and fitting capacity. As illustrated in the right panel of Figure 3, training proceeds in three alternating phases whose trainable parameter budget ebbs and flows like tide: an ebb phase freezes the backbone and updates only lightweight LoRA adapter (a narrow network), whereas flood phase unfreezes the entire model (a wide network). In parallel, we perturb the training input with DINOMAC adversarial noise Qu et al. (2026a) whose intensity is progressively increased from light to medium and finally to relatively heavy, discouraging the memorization of trivially easy samples and improving robustness. Adaptation Ebb. In the first phase, we attach LoRA adapter to the officially pretrained Qwen3.5 backbone and fine-tune only the adapter on an initial portion (15M) of the data under light noise. This phase acts as low-cost warm-up that rapidly adapts the general-purpose pretrained model to the forgery detection task. Meanwhile, freezing the backbone parameters effectively prevents catastrophic forgetting, so that the model keeps access to its acquired world knowledge and learns to exploit it for reasoning about the high-level semantic anomalies present in forged images and videos, yielding stronger generalization. Nevertheless, applying LoRA alone to 2B-parameter model over the full 50M corpus would underfit, since the limited adapter capacity cannot absorb data of such scale and diversity. 8 Full-Parameter Flood. We therefore introduce second phase that releases the full parameter budget. The LoRA weights obtained in the first phase are first merged into the backbone, and the entire model is then fine-tuned on the full corpus under medium noise. With the greatest degree of freedom, this phase offers the strongest fitting capacity for the large-scale heterogeneous corpus. Importantly, because the first phase has already sufficiently adapted the model to forgery detection, training rarely produces large destructive gradients, and catastrophic forgetting is largely avoided. The strengthened DINOMAC adversarial noise further prevents the model from directly memorizing easy samples and enhances robustness. Hard-Sample Ebb. After the flood phase, the model has mastered the majority of the corpus, yet small number of hard samplestogether with newly collected onesremain under-fitted. We therefore freeze the backbone once more and attach fresh LoRA adapter, which is fine-tuned on the new and hard samples under heavy noise. This final ebb phase brings three benefits. First, adapteronly optimization drastically reduces the cost of continued training. Second, the restricted parameter budget acts as an implicit regularizer, preventing the model from overfitting to the easy samples that have already been sufficiently fitted. Third, it steers the model to adapt to the new samples on top of the general features learned by the backbone, rather than overfitting to idiosyncratic visual patterns; the heavy DINOMAC adversarial noise further suppresses overfitting to easy samples. The model obtained after this third phase is taken as our final model. 2.3 Modality Synergism Modality dilemma. Spatial and temporal evidence both exist in video forgery, yet they do not always co-occur strongly within single sample. From the models perspective, the two input modalities correspond to two distinct feature-acquisition pathways. Encoding each frame as an independent image lets the vision encoder concentrate on the spatial texture of individual frames, preserving fine-grained intra-frame artifacts such as generation fingerprints and boundary discontinuities, but discards inter-frame dynamics. Encoding the clip natively as video recovers the temporal context required by evidence such as flickering and motion inconsistency, but at the cost of dispersing attention over redundant temporal tokens and weakening the response to subtle per-frame traces. Since which pathway carries stronger evidence is sample-dependent and unknown priori, any fixed modality can only be optimal in expectation. We therefore cast the modality choice as per-sample inference-time decision, which in turn requires reliable, training-free measure of how confident each modalitys prediction is for the given sample. To this end, we propose Modality Synergism, which tackles the dilemma from both the optimization side and the inference side, via joint modality training and entropy-based test adaptation, respectively. sections.title: 3 Training Data Construction
sections.content: 3.1 Overall We train our vision-forensics foundation model on massive, heterogeneous corpus designed to span broad spectrum of manipulation techniques, forgery granularities, and content modalities. As depicted in Figure 5, this 50M-sample training dataset is constructed by aggregating heterogeneous data sources and deploying dedicated, automated generation pipelines. Provenance-wise, our corpus integrates three primary tiers: public datasets, engine-synthesized data, and manually curated in-thewild attack samples. Functionally, the dataset spans nine distinct forensic domains: AI-generated images, DeepFake faces, tampered documents, forged natural images, face anti-spoofing (images and videos), document anti-spoofing (images and videos), and AI-generated videos. 3.2 Self-Synthesized Data Besides manually forged and annotated data, our private self-synthesized data are mainly sourced from Creative Proposer++ and Agent-based Data Generation pipelines: Creative Proposer++ Pipeline. critical step in constructing large-scale datasets for vision forensics is obtaining high-quality, diverse prompts to guide media generators. Existing syntheticdata methods suffer from significant domain gap: simplistic or random prompts yield unrealistic outputs that lack the semantic plausibility of real-world forgeries. To address this, as illustrated in Figure 5, we introduce Creative Proposer++, novel pipeline that automatically generates diverse, high-quality instructions for synthetic media generation. Built upon the Creative Proposer pipeline Qu et al. (2026d), Creative Proposer++ extends it from images to videos. Specifically, we prompt multimodal large language models (MLLMs), such as Qwen3.5-32B and GPT-5.5, to produce detailed textual description of real-world image or video with the instruction: Describe this image/video in detail so that can prompt an image/video generation model to generate the very same image/video. This prompt elicits rich descriptions that capture subtle visual elements, which are then fed to image or video generators (e.g., GPT-Image-2, SeeDance 2.5) to synthesize realistic counterfeits. Moreover, inherent recognition errors of the MLLMs are leveraged as natural form of text-content counterfeiting, further enhancing data diversity. This design brings two key advantages. First, each synthesized sample reproduces the content of its real-world source, so the real and fake counterparts are semantically aligned by construction. Such alignment naturally prevents the forgery detector from overfitting to semantic or content cues irrelevant to the forgery task, and instead compels it to focus on forgery-relevant evidence such as generation traces and artifacts, thereby substantially improving generalization to unseen forgeries. Second, because the prompts are distilled directly from real-world media, the synthesized data inherit diversity on par with that of the original data, avoiding the limited diversity typically caused by conventional synthesis approaches that rely on handcrafted or template-based prompts. Agent-based Data Generation Pipeline. Additionally, to support data-centric training, we build an agent-based data generation pipeline, as shown in Figure 5. After DefakerOne2 is trained on the data pool, its failure cases are collected and sent to an agent-assisted refinement module. The agent analyzes these bad cases to identify missing forgery patterns, difficult manipulation types, and domains, and then selects suitable generation or editing models to synthesize targeted samples. The newly generated data are added back to the training pool for the next round of optimization. Through this loop of training, agent-based bad-case analysis, data synthesis, and re-training, DefakerOne2 can continuously adapt to evolving forgery methods. Although the same agent-assisted refinement framework is applied across multiple domains, its execution process differs according to the characteristics of each domain. We describe these domain-specific pipeline designs in the next subsection. 3.3 Statistics 3.3.1 AI-Generated Images The training corpus for the AI-generated images domain comprises approximately 16M samples. This includes 8M public samples sourced from the official training splits of DiffusionForensics (Wang et al., 2023), CommunityForensics (Park and Owens, 2025), GenImage (Zhu et al., 2023), LAION (Schuhmann et al., 2022), and ForenSynths (Wang et al., 2020), together with 5.3M video frames extracted via Ada-FPS and 2.7M privately curated samples. In addition, we maintain an extensive pool of commercial APIs and open-source generative/editing models. Upon the release of new AIGC model, our automated agent dynamically queries the corresponding API or engine, pairs targeted prompts with source images, and synthesizes novel samples in high-throughput batches.

sections.content: To systematically benchmark forensic detection capabilities against frontier AI-Generated Content (AIGC) video engines under high-stakes, real-world conditions, we establish the Realistic Rumor Video Benchmark (RRVBench). RRVBench comprises 1, 319 authentic videos sourced from RABench Liang et al. (2026) and 11, 000 synthetic videos produced by 11 modern generative architectures. To reflect the realistic distribution of accessible generative tools, we evaluate both state-of-the-art closed-source and open-source generators: Closed-Source Engines (2, 500 videos): SeeDance-2.5 SeeDance2.5 Team (2026) (700 videos), Happyhorse-1.1 HappyHorse1.1 Team (2026) (400 videos), Vidu2-Image Vidu2Image Team (2026) (400 videos), Wan-2.6-Flash Wan2.6 Team (2026) (400 videos), Wan2.6 Wan2.6 Team (2026) (200 videos), Kling-V3 Video KlingV3 Team (2026) (200 videos), and Kling-V3-Omni Video KlingV3Omni Team (2026) (200 videos). Generation Pipeline and Semantic Bias Mitigation. persistent vulnerability of synthetic benchmarks is the confounding effect of semantic disparity between real and generated distributions. Following the Creative Proposer++ paradigm described above, we mitigate this by using Qwen3.532B Qwen3.5 Team (2026) to extract granular semantic descriptions from authentic source videos. These descriptions subsequently serve as conditioning prompts for the target video generators. This semantic-matching strategy ensures that detectors are evaluated purely on synthesis artifacts rather than high-level contextual or thematic cues. Target Domains and Evaluation Protocol. RRVBench specifically targets critical, high-impact rumor domains, including military actions, political events, civil unrest, and public health emergencies (representative examples are shown in Figure 6). For the evaluation protocol, each generator subset is paired against the complete, unified authentic dataset (1, 319 videos). sections.content: 5.1 Implementation Details We employ the pre-trained Qwen3.5-2B Qwen3.5 Team (2026) as the backbone and initialize the DINOMAC-based Qu et al. (2026a) Anomaly Magnifier with official DINOv3-Large Siméoni et al. (2025) weights. For the Qwen3.5-2B backbone, we adopt LoRA Hu et al. (2022) fine-tuning (rank = 64, α = 128) during the Adaptation Ebb (Stage 1) and Hard-Sample Ebb (Stage 3), using batch size of 1,280 and learning rate decayed from 1 104 to 0. In the Full-Parameter Flood stage (Stage 2), we conduct full-model tuning on the layers targeted by LoRA with batch size of 640 and learning rate decayed from 1 105 to 0. Experiments are distributed across 320 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with an L2-norm gradient clipping threshold of 1.0. The three stages utilize approximately 15M, 40M, and 40M samples, respectively. We apply random sampling strategy across CommunityForensics Park and Owens (2025), LAION Schuhmann et al. (2022), DiffusionForensics Wang et al. (2023), GenImage Zhu et al. (2023), ScaleDF Wang et al. (2025b), DF40 Yan et al. (2024b), MFFI Miao et al. (2025), and proprietary datasets to balance domain distributions and ensure mutually disjoint splits across stages. This disjoint split constraint applies only to the datasets listed above; all other datasets are shared across stages. standard threshold of 0.5 is used for binarization. For the Qwen3.5-2B backbone, dynamic image resolutions range from 512 512 to 1024 2352 pixels, while video inputs are capped at 4 frames and 256 visual tokens. For the Anomaly Magnifier, input resolutions are randomly sampled from 768 768 to 1536 1536 pixels. Prior to joint end-to-end training in the final stage, the magnifier is continually pre-trained on forgery localization data for 20 epochs with its mask decoder, with batch size of 768 and learning rate scheduled from 1 104 to 0. Image-level Detection Comparison 5.2 In this subsection, we benchmark our model against forensic-specific detectors across four domains (DeepFake, AIGC, document, and natural images). (2023), MVP Yu et al. (2025) and LCDF Li et al. (2025b), as well as models for the video anti-forgery domain, including BusterX Wen et al. (2025a), VideoVeritas Tan et al. (2026a), Ivy-xDetector Jiang et al. (2026a) and Veritas Tan et al. (2026b). We further include the forensicspecific models from the four image detection domains (DeepFake, AIGC, document and natural images), namely DTD Qu et al. (2023), FFDN Chen et al. (2024h), TruFor Guillaro et al. (2023), CDFA Lin et al. (2024), Effort Yan et al. (2024a), DRCT Chen et al. (2024a) and ForensicMoE Fang et al. (2025), as well as our previous version DeFakerOne Team (2026). For models incapable of processing video inputs directly, each video clip is decomposed into individual frames and evaluated at the image level under unified protocol, ensuring fair and direct comparison across detectors from all three domains: anti-spoofing, video forensics, and still-image forensics. 5.3.1 Comparison on Classic Physical and Digital Forgery Benchmarks Image-level accuracy comparisons are reported in Table 10 (non-MLLMs) and Table 11 (MLLMs), and the corresponding Half Total Error Rate (HTER) comparisons, where lower is better, in Table 12 (non-MLLMs) and Table 13 (MLLMs). The eight benchmarks jointly span classic physical spoofing and modern digital video forgery: CASIA-FASD, DLC2021, GenBuster++, GenBuster-ID, GenBuster-OOD, LOKI, SCVD and VideoPhy2. Accuracy. DefakerOne2 attains the best result on 7 of the 8 benchmarks, the single exception being CASIA-FASD, where the dedicated face anti-spoofing detector FLIP remains ahead (98.5 vs. 90.3). It reaches an average accuracy of 96.0%, outperforming version 1 by 33.3% and surpassing the strongest external vision baseline, MVP (69.8), by 26.2%; against the best forensic MLLM, VideoVeritas (68.3), the margin is 27.7%. The improvement over version 1 is not marginal but structural: it exceeds 25 points on five benchmarks and reaches +69.2 on SCVD (28.1 97.3) and +60.5 on VideoPhy2 (38.9 99.4), the two suites on which version 1 performs at or below the chance level. Version 2 additionally saturates DLC2021 (99.9), GenBuster-ID (99.9) and GenBusterOOD (99.6), showing that the gain does not come from over-fitting the in-distribution generators: the OOD split, on which every competing method degrades to between 44.7 and 90.2, is handled almost perfectly, and the residual difficulty concentrates on GenBuster++ (88.6), the in-the-wild split that mixes compression and post-processing perturbations with the forgery itself. The baseline families fail for different reasons. Most image-domain forensic models simply do not transfer to video frames: DTD (35.0), TruFor (37.5), ForensicMoE (40.6), CDFA (47.3), LCDF (55.4) and DRCT (55.5) all remain within few points of random guessing, and DTD collapses to 0.0 on VideoPhy2, indicating that the tampering cues they rely onsplicing boundaries, copymove residuals, text-region inconsistenciesare absent from frame whose entire content is synthesized rather than locally edited. The physical anti-spoofing models transfer better on the benchmarks that match their training domain (FLIP on CASIA-FASD, MVP on GenBusterOOD) but do not generalize beyond them, with FLIP fluctuating between 49.1 and 98.5 across the suite. The forensic MLLMs, despite their reasoning capability, are equally limited: BusterX (52.5), Ivy-xDetector (53.5) and Veritas (63.2) stay close to chance on SCVD (28.7/26.0/28.6) and CASIA-FASD (25.8/33.7/63.7), and only VideoVeritas exhibits usable level of robustness, yet with pronounced per-generator variance (91.1 on VideoPhy2 but 30.8 on SCVD). HTER. The HTER tables sharpen these observations, because the metric averages the error on the real and on the fake class and therefore cannot be inflated by biased decision threshold. 23 DefakerOne2 again leads on 7 of the 8 benchmarks with an average HTER of 5.0, against 29.4 for version 1, 31.6 for the best external vision baseline (MVP) and 27.9 for the best forensic MLLM (VideoVeritas). In relative terms this is an 83.0% reduction of the error with respect to version 1 and an 84.2% reduction with respect to MVP. Five benchmarks are driven to an essentially error-free regimeDLC2021 (0.1), GenBuster-ID (0.1), VideoPhy2 (0.3), GenBuster-OOD (0.4) and SCVD (1.8)and even the two hardest ones, GenBuster++ (11.4) and CASIA-FASD (18.9), remain below every competitor, with the sole exceptions of FLIP (2.3) and MVP (4.6) on CASIA-FASD. More importantly, HTER exposes systematic bias that the accuracy tables conceal. Several baselines obtain moderate accuracy while their average HTER sits at roughly 35 or higher, i.e. they classify one of the two classes much better than the other: DTD (35.0 accuracy / 50.0 HTER), TruFor (37.5 / 51.0), ForensicMoE (40.6 / 45.1), CDFA (47.3 / 48.0 HTER) and LCDF (55.4 / 43.1) belong to this group, as do the MLLMs Ivy-xDetector (53.5 / 42.6) and BusterX (52.5 / 34.8). DefakerOne2 is also the only method whose two metrics agree with each other across the suite: the mean discrepancy between its accuracy and its balanced accuracy stays within one point on seven of the eight benchmarks (average 1.3 points, with CASIA-FASD the single exception at 9.2), whereas every competitor deviates by 3.1 to 15.1 points on average. Its verdicts are therefore balanced between real and forged clips rather than obtained by collapsing onto the majority class, property that accuracy alone would not reveal and that is indispensable for deployment, where the real/fake proportion of the incoming traffic is unknown. Summary. Across both metrics and both competitor families, the results support two conclusions. First, neither physical anti-spoofing models nor AI-generated-video reasoning models, and neither still-image forensic detectors nor forensic MLLMs, cover the full spectrum of classic physical and digital video forgeries on their own; each family is competent only on the subset that resembles its training distribution. Second, DefakerOne2 closes this gap with single set of weights, improving the average accuracy by 33.3 points and cutting the average HTER by 24.4 points over version 1, which shows that the unified multi-domain training together with the modality-synergistic inference transfers to the video level rather than being confined to the image domains. 5.3.2 Comparison on RABench Table 14 reports zero-shot AUC comparisons on RA-Bench against specialized image and video forensic detectors. Evaluated image-based methods include CNNSpot Wang et al. (2020), NPR Tan et al. (2024), UnivFD Ojha et al. (2023), and ForgeLens Chen et al. Consistently, DefakerOne2 sets superior benchmark across all 11 sub-benchmarks. Our 2Bparameter model outperforms the substantially larger 7B-parameter video forensic models BusterX, Ivy-xDetector, and VideoVeritas by 38.9%, 27.5%, and 25.5%, respectively, while exceeding DeFakerOne by massive 43.0% margin and the best non-MLLM baseline DRCT (62.1) by 33.2%. This exceptional generalization confirms the models zero-shot robustness against unseen, contemporary video synthesizers, underscoring its real-world utility in countering viral synthetic rumors. RRVBench is, of the three video evaluations, the harshest test of generalization, and the baselines behave accordingly. Nine of the ten non-MLLM detectors score within 48.256.2, statistically indistinguishable from the 50 of random classifier; DTD is exactly 50.0 on every generator and TruFor varies by less than two points (49.150.7), which is the signature of detector that has no usable evidence at all on this data rather than one that is merely inaccurate. Version 2 keeps the image-domain advantage and repairs both weaknesses: it lifts physical image forgery from 50.7 to 87.2 (+36.5), physical video forgery from 50.7 to 95.8 (+45.1), and the RRVBench row from 52.3 to 95.3 (+43.0). First, the competitor averages are almost flat across domains, while their per-domain rankings rotate: model that is best on one row can be near-chance on another. Second, the spread within our own rows is small (87.296.7 in the image block, 95.396.1 in the video block), which means the unified training does not trade one domain against another. Together these observations support the claim of this work: single 2B-parameter model, trained once and inferred with the modality-synergistic protocol, provides detection capability that is simultaneously state-of-the-art in every domain examined and balanced across them, whereas the existing landscape requires one specialized detector per domain and still leaves physical forgery and unseen video synthesizers unsolved. The three Ours columns on the right are the cumulative checkpoints produced after the adaptation ebb, the full-parameter flood and the hard-sample ebb, respectively, so that consecutive columns isolate the marginal contribution of each phase. Neither static parameterization dominates. The first observation concerns the two baselines themselves. All-Full improves the image average over All-LoRA by only +0.5 points (87.3 87.8) while losing 0.6 points on video (93.6 93.0), leaving the two regimes statistically indistinguishable overall (means of 90.45 and 90.40). This trade-off is exactly the dilemma analyzed in Sec. 2.3: enlarging the parameter budget buys fitting capacity for the heterogeneous majority at the price of eroding the pretrained knowledge that the temporal branch relies on, whereas restricting the budget preserves that knowledge but cannot absorb 50M-scale training corpus. The fact that the two extremes land on the same overall level, but through complementary image/video strengths, indicates that the bottleneck is not the amount of trainable parameters but the schedule by which they are released. Stage 1 quantifies the cost of the constrained warm-up. After the adaptation ebb the model reaches 84.6 on images and 91.8 on video, i.e. 2.7 and 1.8 points below All-LoRA. This gap is expected rather than contradictory: Stage 1 consumes only the initial 15M portion of the corpus under light DINOMAC noise, whereas All-LoRA is trained on all 50M samples, and its adapter is therefore asked to cover three times the data with the same capacity. The comparison is nonetheless informative, as it confirms empirically the underfitting argument that motivates the flood phasea purely adapter-based recipe, however long it is trained, saturates well below the level that the full parameter budget can reach. Stage 1 should consequently be read as an initialization rather than as candidate final model. Stage 2 isolates the benefit of the ebb initialization. Merging the Stage-1 adapter into the backbone and unfreezing all parameters under medium noise lifts the model to 88.4 / 94.2, the first setting that surpasses both static baselines on both modalities. Since Stage 2 and All-Full share the same trainable parameterization and the same full corpus, the +0.6 (image) and +1.2 (video) margin is attributable to the preceding adapter warm-up alone: having already been steered towards the forgery-detection objective, the backbone enters the high-capacity phase in region of the loss landscape where destructive gradients are rare, so full fine-tuning adds capacity without triggering the catastrophic forgetting that degrades All-Full. The jump from Stage 1 (+3.8 image, +2.4 video) further shows that the released parameter budget is indeed converted into fitting power for the hard portion of the corpus. 30 Table 21 Ablation of the proposed Modality Synergism. The final hard-sample ebb re-freezes the backbone, attaches fresh adapter and trains it on the new and hard samples under heavy noise, yielding 90.9 / 95.7 and the best result in every column of the table. The most stringent comparison is against All-LoRA, because both settings end with adapter-only optimization over comparable amount of data: the tide schedule nevertheless delivers +3.6 points on images and +2.1 points on video, which in relative error terms corresponds to 28.3% reduction of the image error (12.7 9.1) and 32.8% reduction of the video error (6.4 4.3). Against All-Full the margins are +3.1 and +2.7, i.e. 25.4% and 38.6% error reduction. Identical parameter budgets and identical data therefore produce markedly different detectors, and the difference can only come from the order in which capacity is granted: the narrow adapter of Stage 3 operates on top of features already generalized by the flood phase, which is what prevents it from re-fitting the easy majority that All-LoRA memorizes from scratch. 5.6.2 Ablation on Modality Synergism Table 21 isolates the inference-side component of Modality Synergism. The first two columns force the same jointly trained network to single input pathwayAda-FPS frame sequence or native clipand therefore characterize the two feature-acquisition pathways described in Sec. 2.3. The third and fourth columns report the fraction of test samples for which the entropy criterion of Eq. (9) selects each pathway, and the last column gives the accuracy of the routed predictor. Averaged over the ten benchmarks, the frame pathway attains 91.6, the video pathway 93.5, and the routed predictor 95.9, i.e. +4.3 and +2.4 points over the respective fixed choices. In relative terms the error rate is nearly halved with respect to the frame pathway (8.4 4.1, 50% reduction) and reduced by 37.4% with respect to the video pathway (6.5 4.1). Since both single-modality columns are produced by the same set of weights, this improvement is attributable to the entropy-based test adaptation alone, without any additional training or learned routing module. The two pathways are complementary, not ordered. If one modality were uniformly stronger, fixed choice would be optimal and per-sample routing would be pointless. The table refutes this directly. The frame pathway is decisive on RABench (98.2 vs. 87.4), RRVBench (97.6 vs. 85.2) and VideoPhy2 Test (99.4 vs. 95.6), whereas the video pathway is decisive on SCVD (95.1 vs. 71.9), GenBuster++ (88.4 vs. 72.2) and LOKI (95.1 vs. 89.3). The large inter-modality gaps reach 3.8 points on VideoPhy2 Test and 16.2 points on GenBuster++, and on six of the ten benchmarks 31 the weaker pathway falls below 90. This is the empirical counterpart of the modality dilemma: benchmarks whose forgeries are frame-localtext and logo-level edits in RABench and RRVBench, per-frame generation fingerprintsare damaged by dispersing attention over redundant temporal tokens, while benchmarks whose forgeries are trajectory-levelphysically implausible motion in LOKI, whole-clip generative statistics in GenBuster++leave almost no intra-frame trace to be found. The selection ratios confirm that the entropy criterion perceives this structure: they span from 5.4% (SCVD) to 95.4% (DLC2021) of frame selections and track the stronger pathway on nine of the ten benchmarks, including the two extremes. Yet the average ratio is 50.0%/50.0%, which shows that the routing is not the expression of global preference but genuinely sample-adaptive decision that happens to balance out over the suite. Routing is super-additive on the hard benchmarks. On four benchmarks the routed predictor exceeds both fixed modalities: SCVD (71.9/95.1 97.3), GenBuster OOD (97.2/98.5 99.6), CASIA-FASD (90.0/89.8 90.3) and GenBuster++ (72.2/88.4 88.6). Such result cannot be explained by selecting the better of two predictors, and it verifies the design of Modality Synergism at the level of individual samples: within one benchmark, the modality carrying the stronger evidence varies from sample to sample, so mixture of the two pathways covers strictly larger region of the sample space than either pathway alone. The effect is largest exactly where single pathway is weakestSCVD gains 25.4 points over the frame pathway and 2.2 over the video pathway, and GenBuster++ gains 16.4 and 0.2 respectivelywhich is the intended behaviour of router that is supposed to pay off most when the fixed-modality error is highest. Aggregating the per-benchmark stronger pathway gives an upper reference of 96.2; the routed predictor reaches 95.9 and hence recovers 93.5% of the gap between that reference and the frame pathway. The routing thus operates close to the best static per-benchmark choice while requiring no benchmark identity at test time. Interaction with joint modality training. The inference-side adaptation is only meaningful if both pathways are reliable in the first place, which is the role of the dual loss in Eq. (6): optimizing the shared backbone against the same label under both input representations forces it to internalize spatial and temporal evidence simultaneously, so that either pathway can be invoked at test time. The fact that the frame pathway reaches 99.9 on DLC2021 and GenBuster ID while the video pathway reaches 95.1 on both SCVD and LOKI, within one and the same set of weights, is consistent with this objective. The Ada-FPS strategy complements it on the data side: without per-source rate adaptation, few abundant video sources would consume most of the frame budget, and the frame pathway would be under-trained precisely on the scarce sources for which it is the informative one. We note that Table 21 varies the inference-time modality only and thus does not separately quantify the contribution of Eq. (6) and of Ada-FPS; ablating them would require training single-modality variants of the network, which we leave for future work. Even so, the two components are not independent in effect: routing rule that selects between an untrained and trained pathway would merely recover the trained one, and the observed super-additivity on SCVD, GenBuster-OOD, GenBuster++ and CASIA-FASD is only attainable when both pathways are individually competent. 5.6.3 Ablation on Decoding Hyper-parameters To assess the inference stability of DefakerOne2, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on decoding hyperparameters, with results presented in Table 22. Regarding random seed variations, we evaluate three distinct seeds (42, 1024, and 4096) and observe virtually identical performance across all configurations, with image accuracy stable at 90.891.0% and video accuracy consistently ranging from 95.6% to 95.7%. This negligible variance demonstrates that our unified training paradigm effectively eliminates sensitivity to initialization stochasticity, ensuring reproducible 32 Table 22 Ablation study of decoding hyperparameters. Image-level detection task Model Dataset/ AUC DefakerOne MFFI MFFI-Distorted 96.1 76.4 -20.5% DefakerOne2 MFFI MFFI-Distorted 97.3 90.1 -7.4% predictions in deployment scenarios. We further examine temperature scaling, critical parameter controlling prediction diversity in generative models. Across temperatures ranging from 0.0 (highly deterministic) to 1.0 (increased stochasticity), DeFakerOne2 maintains remarkable stability with accuracy fluctuating within merely 0.1 percentage points (90.991.0%) and the scores remaining stable at 95.595.7%. The minimal performance degradation at elevated temperatures, where one might expect increased prediction variance, substantiates that the model has learned robust forensic decision boundaries rather than relying on brittle spurious correlations. These results collectively establish that DefakerOne2 delivers consistent, reliable outputs across diverse operational configurations, critical prerequisite for forensic applications where verdict reproducibility carries legal and evidentiary significance. 5.6.4 Robustness evaluation We perform image-level classification robustness evaluation on MFFI dataset, which has an official robustness evaluation sub-set, termed as MFFI-Distorted. The MFFI-Distorted sub-set simulates real-world degradation processes during data propagation, with randomly embedded multi-level interference factors including blur processing, noise interference, color distortion, geometric deformation, sharpening artifacts, compression distortion, and adversarial perturbations. Notably, our training pipeline does not mimic the MFFI official distortions specifically and our distortions have gap with the MFFI official distortions. Despite this, our model still shows significantly improved robustness. As shown in Table 23, the version 1 DefakerOne model undergoes 20.5% AUC degradation on MFFI-Distorted (from 96.1 to 76.4), while our DefakerOne2 maintains an AUC score above 90 on MFFI-Distorted. The results indicate that our DefakerOne2 posseses strong robustness under realistic and challenging conditions, making it more reliable for practical deployment.

We first examine the contribution of the auxiliary encoder by comparing settings (a), (b) and (c). Averaged over all 14 benchmarks, the pixel-level F1 rises from 59.8 in the baseline to 66.0 with ConvNeXt-Large Anomaly Magnifier and further to 77.7 with the DINOMAC Anomaly Magnifier, indicating that the vision encoder of the MLLM alone is insufficient for dense forensic prediction and that an auxiliary pixel-oriented branch is indispensable. Adding generic auxiliary encoder is not enough. Setting (b) reveals clear dichotomy between the two blocks. On document benchmarks, the ConvNeXt-Large branch brings consistent and substantial improvement, raising the average from 58.3 to 73.0, with the largest gains on datasets whose tampering is region-scoped and boundary-driven (DocTamper-SCD, 34.6 68.4; DocTamperTest, 41.9 73.9; RTM, 27.2 46.2). On natural images, however, the same module degrades the average from 61.9 to 56.7, and COVERAGE, CocoGlide, AutoSplice, NIST16 and Columbia all fall below the baseline, with COVERAGE dropping by 21.1 points. The reason is that ConvNeXt-Large is pre-trained with image-level classification supervision, so its features encode semantic saliency rather than forensic inconsistency. When such features are concatenated with the MLLM representation, the decoder gains capacity but no new evidence: it simply becomes better at segmenting whatever region looks prominent, which helps on splicing-style document tampering yet over-segments benign texture and fails on manipulations that leave no semantic cue, such as the diffusion-based inpainting of CocoGlide and AutoSplice. The only natural benchmark that benefits (CASIAv1, 79.0 87.6) is precisely one dominated by obvious object-level splicing, which is consistent with this explanation. 34 forensically tuned encoder turns the extra capacity into gains. Replacing the ConvNeXt-Large backbone with DINOMAC in setting (c) improves the document average by 6.1 points (to 79.1) and the natural average by 19.2 points (to 75.9), removing the regression introduced in (b) and lifting 12 of the 14 benchmarks above the baseline. The improvements are concentrated where the traces are low-level rather than semantic: COVERAGE (50.9 83.3), NIST16 (41.4 73.2), AutoSplice (36.8 59.8) and CocoGlide (34.0 55.9). This verifies our motivation for the DINOMAC backbone: the self-supervised DINOv3 representation provides dense, patch-aligned features suitable for pixel-wise prediction, while the LoRA adapter and the forensic training strategy redirect these features towards artifacts such as inconsistent blur, resampling and boundary discontinuity, instead of object semantics. The two exceptions are informative as well. On T-SROIE the DINO backbone is slightly behind both the baseline and the ConvNeXt variant (89.7 87.2), which we attribute to the coarse patchification of ViT-style encoders that discards the stroke-level high-frequency detail on which small receipt-text tampering depends, whereas the hierarchical stem of ConvNeXt preserves it. On Columbia, small splicing-only benchmark where the baseline is already close to saturation (94.9), the additional branch mainly introduces redundant features. Both cases are limited in magnitude and do not offset the overall trend, and the average gain of setting (c) over the baseline is 20.8 points on documents and 14.0 points on natural images. 5.7.2 Ablation on MLLM Calibration Setting (d) adds the calibration loop of Eqs. (1)(3) on top of setting (c). The loop introduces no trainable parameter, yet it improves the document average from 79.1 to 79.5 and the natural average from 75.9 to 78.1, i.e., +1.2 points over all 14 benchmarks, and it attains the best on 7 of them. The gains concentrate on subtle and diffuse manipulations. Eight benchmarks improve, with an average gain of +3.3 points, and the largest ones are CocoGlide (55.9 65.6), AutoSplice (59.8 67.4), RTM (51.7 56.5) and DanceText (59.6 61.7). These are exactly the cases in which the pixel branch alone under-segments: generative inpainting leaves no splicing boundary, so the anomaly map is broad but of low confidence, and text-level edits alter only few strokes within large authentic background. fixed cut-off suppresses most of these weak responses, whereas the global branch correctly identifies such images as forged. With 1, the dynamic threshold is lowered to τ = 0.25, the admissible region is enlarged, and the diffuse responses that were already ranked correctly but sitting below the neutral boundary are recovered. The calibration therefore acts as recall-oriented prior on hard samples, and the improvement is largest where the gap between (c) and the achievable upper bound is widest. Summary. The two ablations are complementary. The Anomaly Magnifier supplies forensic evidence that the MLLM vision encoder cannot provide and accounts for the bulk of the improvement (59.8 77.7), whereas the calibration loop exploits the global judgment to re-balance the localization decision boundary and contributes further +1.2 points at zero parameter cost, mainly by recovering manipulations that are visible globally but weak locally. 5.8 t-SNE visualization and Analyses To inspect what the unified multi-domain training actually writes into the backbone, we project with t-SNE Van der Maaten and Hinton (2008) the hidden states of the last transformer layer preceding the LLM classification head, i.e. the representation from which the single Real/Fake decision token is decoded. Authenticity is not separable axis of the projected space. Within every cluster, real (label=0) and fake (label=1) markers interpenetrate rather than occupying two disjoint halves: in C1, the 128 natural-image samples (nat), of which the model misclassifies 21.1%, co-locate with the 706 forgeries of semantically adjacent domains, and in C3 authentic samples sit inside the frameaigc manifold rather than beside itthe same region hosts aigc at 100.0% accuracy and nat at only 71.7%. Misclassified samples (yellow and red markers) are likewise scattered through the cluster interiors instead of concentrating at cluster peripheries or at realfake contact zones, which shows that the errors are not confined to thin ambiguous band that better decision threshold could remove. The binary verdict is thus recovered by the classification head from domain-conditioned cues, without any globally linear Real/Fake direction in the last-layer representationa property that also explains why the entropy-based test adaptation of Sec. 2.3, which compares modality-wise certainty rather than shared margin, is needed at inference time. Implications for future optimization. The two structural weaknesses abovesoft, overlapping domain manifolds and an implicit authenticity boundarysuggest two direct remedies, both acting on the same last-layer hidden states. First, cluster-aware metric learning objective: augmenting the detection loss with supervised contrastive or center-plus-margin loss whose class index is the forensic type label (or pseudo-cluster assignment) would force each domain to collapse into compact, well-separated manifold, reducing the probability that sample is mis-routed into foreign cluster and suffers the accuracy penalty quantified above. This is particularly warranted for the content-diverse flags that currently lack single attractoraigc and natwhose dispersion, rather than their intrinsic difficulty, accounts for large part of their accuracy loss; type-conditioned objective could grant them the compactness that deepfake obtains for free from its face appearance prior. Second, an explicit authenticity margin: complementing the domain-level structure with binary contrastive or additive angular margin term between real and fake representations, applied within each domain cluster, would sharpen the Real/Fake decision surface that is currently only implicit in the head weights. Together, these objectives would turn the observed soft manifolds into geometry in which both which forensic domain and real or fake are linearly readable from the representation, and we expect them to convert directly into closure of the per-flag, per-cluster accuracy gaps reported in Table 25. We leave the exploration of such structured representation objectives to future work. 5.9 Evaluation on In-house Data To evaluate DefakerOne2s potential on defending real-world attacks in-depth, we fine-tune different models on the same in-house data and evaluate model performance on four in-house real-world attack datasets.
