sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we presented Venus-DefakerOne2, to the best of our knowledge the first unified vision anti-forgery foundation model that simultaneously covers the full matrix of {digital, physical} {image, video} forgery. Trained on large-scale corpus of about 50M samples consolidated from public datasets, self-constructed datasets, and manually annotated online-attack samples, our model learns shared fundamental features of vision forgery across content types, forgery forms, and media types, thereby bridging the long-standing fragmentation in which digital image forensics, face anti-spoofing, document fraud detection, and video forensics had been studied in largely separate communities Du et al. (2026a). To tackle the prohibitive training cost and the drastically uneven sample difficulty inherent in such heterogeneous corpus, we proposed Tide-Style Tuning, an alternating three-phase regime that ebbs from LoRA-based adaptation, flows into full-parameter finetuning, and ebbs back to LoRA regularization, reconciling computational efficiency, generalization, and fitting capacity within single training pipeline. To resolve the modality dilemma in video forensics, we proposed Modality Synergism, which aligns the video and frame modalities on both the optimization and inference sides: joint modality training with independent detection losses internalizes both spatial and temporal forensic evidence into the shared backbone, while entropybased test adaptation adaptively routes each sample to the more certain modality at inference time, without any additional training or learned routing module. In addition, we constructed RRVBench, realistic rumor video benchmark populated by fake videos synthesized with the latest closedand open-source generators, substantially narrowing the gap between academic evaluation and real-world AIGC threats. Extensive experiments on 53 visual media forgery detection benchmarks and 14 forgery localization benchmarks demonstrate that Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves state-of-the-art performance across wide spectrum of forgery scenarios, validating the effectiveness of the unified modeling paradigm for vision anti-forgery.

sections.title: 7 Future Work
sections.content: While our DefakerOne2 paradigm successfully establishes unified foundation for full-spectrum vision forensics, the rapid evolution of generative models demands sustained innovation. We identify two primary directions for future research: Scalable Foundation Forensics and Continual Data Engineering. Our primary objective is to scale DefakerOne2 from an isolated framework into versatile forensic foundation model suitable for broad deployment. As demonstrated by our findings, simply scaling raw, homogeneous data yields diminishing returns. Instead, the core challenge lies in architecting automated, high-throughput data pipelines capable of generating high-fidelity, diverse, and representative forensic benchmarks. To keep pace with emergent synthesis techniques, we will integrate continual learning protocols to dynamically update the training distribution while enhancing robustness against open-world perturbations and unseen manipulation artifacts. Agentic Forensics and Hybrid Knowledge Injection. We aim to bridge the gap between static detection and dynamic, evidence-driven reasoning through agentic paradigms. central challenge remains balancing outcome-level supervision (which suffers from label scarcity and lack of interpretability) and process-level supervision (e.g., Chain-of-Thought reasoning, which is currently limited by manual prompt engineering and domain-specific heuristics). We envision hybrid paradigm where multi-modal agents leverage verifiable forensic tools and authentic ground-truth cues, evolving toward explainable and multi-step forensic investigations.

sections.title: 8 Related Works
sections.content: 8.1 Datasets The evolution of visual forensics datasets reflects clear paradigm shift from single-scenario detection toward unified, multi-domain forensics. Early benchmarks were predominantly tailored to specific manipulation types or targetssuch as face swapping, natural image splicing, document text tampering, or full-image synthesis. Consequently, they exhibited strong domain-specific constraints in data sources, annotation formats, task definitions, and evaluation protocols. With the rapid rise of generative foundation models, the boundaries between these forgery domains have become increasingly blurred: datasets for AI-generated image detection now span broader range of contents (from daily scenes to faces and text), while benchmarks for document and natural image tampering have expanded beyond traditional splicing and copy-move operations to generative local editing. Nevertheless, existing datasets remain largely confined to their respective subdomains, lacking unified data foundation capable of supporting the full spectrum of visual forensics. To contextualize these challenges, this section reviews and analyzes representative datasets across each domain. 8.1.1 DeepFake Detection In the DeepFake detection domain, the evolution of benchmark datasets has witnessed clear transition from early low-fidelity face swap samples to high-quality, diversified collections tailored to evaluate model generalization against unseen and complex forgery patterns. As foundational benchmark in DeepFake detection, FaceForensics++ Rossler et al. (2019) is constructed with four typical DeepFake manipulation types and multi-level compression distortions, which establishes universal evaluation standard for verifying the robustness of detection models against common forgery and compression artifacts. To address the overfitting problem caused by conspicuous fixed artifacts in early datasets, Celeb-DF Li et al. (2020) is developed as large-scale highauthenticity dataset with minimized visible manipulation traces, providing more challenging evaluation benchmark to test the generalization ability of detectors against high-fidelity fake samples. As large-scale diverse benchmark for real-scene simulation, the DFDC Dolhansky et al. (2019) dataset incorporates massive video clips from hundreds of actors with varied lighting conditions and facial poses, effectively simulating complex social media video distributions and expanding the diversity and applicability of DeepFake evaluation. Differing from laboratory-synthesized datasets, WildDeepFake Zi et al. (2020) is curated with real-world DeepFake videos collected from open internet platforms, offering practical in-the-wild testbed to validate the outdoor generalization performance of detection models. Targeting fine-grained and specific forgery scenarios, UADFV Li and Lyu (2018) and Fsh Li et al. (2019) are specialized datasets that focus on unique forgery characteristics including inconsistent head pose variations and occlusion-adaptive face swapping, enabling precise analysis of the localized failure cases of existing detectors. DF40 Yan et al. (2024b) significantly advances the diversity of forgery types compared with traditional datasets. It covers 40 distinct deepfake manipulation techniques spanning face swapping, face reenactment, full-face synthesis, and facial editing. Complementing the aforementioned mainstream benchmarks, ScaleDF Wang et al. (2025b) and MFFI Miao et al. (2025) further enrich the dataset system by addressing overlooked research scenarios. As scale-oriented specialized dataset, ScaleDF Wang et al. (2025b) is designed to compensate for the lack of multi-scale facial variation samples in existing benchmarks. It contains 10+ million-scale massive fake videos covering diverse shooting distances and facial scales, enabling systematic evaluation of detectors scale robustness in complex real-world scenarios. As dedicated multi-face forgery benchmark, MFFI Miao et al. (2025) targets the 43 under-explored multi-person manipulation scenarios neglected by most single-face-focused datasets. It integrates diverse multi-face forgery techniques and varied scene layouts, effectively filling the research gap in multi-face DeepFake detection evaluation. Collectively, these diversified datasets drive the continuous advancement of DeepFake detection research, facilitating the development of models capable of capturing subtle blending boundaries, tiny frequency anomalies, and scale/sceneaware forgery features across various generative architectures. 8.1.2 AI-Generated Image Detection The emergence of diffusion models and large-scale generative AI has driven the evolution of forgery datasets toward fully synthetic content, departing from traditional benchmarks centered on localized facial editing. Unlike conventional DeepFake detection that focuses on altered facial regions, modern AI-generated image detection requires identifying global texture inconsistencies and latent-space generative artifacts. As million-scale comprehensive benchmark, GenImage Zhu et al. (2023) pairs real ImageNet samples with synthetic images generated by eight distinct models, supporting systematic evaluation of cross-model generalization for detection algorithms. As an early exploratory benchmark for synthetic forgery detection, ForenSynths Wang et al. (2020) aggregates fake images produced by diverse GAN architectures, laying foundation for training universal synthetic forgery detectors. With the rapid proliferation of diffusion-based generative models, DiffusionForensics Wang et al. (2023) and Chameleon Yan et al. (2025) are proposed as diffusion-specific datasets, dedicated to capturing the unique noise distributions and spectral artifacts inherent to diffusion generation processes. To further simulate realistic and challenging detection scenarios, SynthWildx Cozzolino et al. (2024) and BFree-Online Guillaro et al. (2025) incorporate synthetic images generated by black-box commercial APIs with complex post-processing operations, posing rigorous challenge for real-world detection. Targeting hard-case forgery evaluation, FakeInversion Cazenavette et al. (2024) adopts generative model inversion techniques to construct high-difficulty negative samples, while EvalGEN Chen et al. (2025b) builds standardized evaluation framework to quantitatively assess detection reliability across diverse prompts and artistic styles. Further advancing robust generalization evaluation, HydraFake Tan et al. (2026b) is specifically constructed to simulate complex, multi-pattern generative forgery scenarios, featuring diverse forgery types and subtle hybrid artifacts that evade conventional detection methods. This dataset effectively benchmarks the capability of detectors to mine latent forgery patterns and reason cross-domain inconsistencies, providing critical testbed for generalized pattern-aware forgery detection. Community Forensics Park and Owens (2025) is constructed based on thousands of diverse generative models, covering extremely rich synthetic image distributions to eliminate model-specific detection bias and enhance the universal generalization capability of fake image detectors. Collectively, these diversified datasets shift forensic research focus from localized facial manipulation traces to global statistical and latent-space anomalies, greatly promoting the development of robust, generalizable AI forgery detection models across various generative architectures.

sections.title: 8.1.3 Tampered Document Image Detection
sections.content: Tampered document image detection represents specialized subfield focused on textual consistency, font rendering fidelity, and layout integrity Qu et al. (2024a); Li et al.. This domain demands datasets that capture fine-grained tampering patternssuch as character substitution, copy-paste manipulations, and signature forgeryto support the development of robust forensic analysis models. DocTamper Qu et al. (2023) is representative large-scale dataset comprising diverse tampering types applied to photographed documents, with pixel-level annotation masks provided for tampering 44 localization tasks. Building upon optical character recognition (OCR) benchmarks, T-SROIE Wang et al. (2022b) and Tampered IC13 Wang et al. (2022a) adapt receipt and natural scene text datasets by introducing synthetic manipulations, serving as standard testbeds to evaluate the robustness of text-based forensic models in unconstrained visual environments. Complementing these scene text forensics benchmarks, Open-Set Text Forensics (OSTF) dataset Qu et al. (2025a) re-examines the problem of scene text tampering detection against the backdrop of advanced generative AI technologies. It addresses the limitations of conventional synthetic tampering by incorporating more realistic and semantically coherent generative text tampering cases in natural scenes, offering more challenging evaluation protocol for modern detectors facing AI-driven forgery threats. Datasets including RTM Luo et al. (2025), SACP Alibaba Security (2020) and RIFLC Alibaba Cloud Tianchi (2024) are specifically designed to bridge the domain gap between synthetically generated tampering samples and real-world scanned document artifacts, enhancing the practical generalizability of detection models. Moving beyond pixel-level tampering localization, TextForensicsReasoning (TFR) Qu et al. (2026c) introduces reasoning-centric benchmark for tampered text analysis. Unlike conventional datasets that prioritize positional annotation, TFR frames text forensics as cognitive reasoning task: models are required to not only locate tampered regions but also infer the rationality of text content, contextual coherence, and logical consistency Chen et al. (2024e), thereby reinforcing the high-level reasoning capability of forensic systems. With the proliferation of AI image generation models, benchmarks targeting AI-counterfeited text have emerged as critical branch of this field. DanceText Qu et al. (2026d) provides comprehensive and diversified benchmark for detecting various AI-generated fake text images. It covers broad spectrum of text formsspanning both structured document text and unconstrained scene textwith diverse counterfeiting strategies and visual styles, enabling thorough assessment of detectors cross-scenario generalization ability. SynCred-Bench Yang et al. (2026a) is another recent benchmark featuring realistic document images synthesized by the state-of-the-art GPT-Image-2 model, with specific focus on evaluating detector performance on challenging credential document forgery cases. Beyond general image forensics tasks, these datasets collectively emphasize both the semantic coherence of text content and the physical properties of ink and paper, making them indispensable foundational resources for developing reliable models dedicated to verifying the authenticity of official records, identity documents and legal documents. 8.1.4 Manipulated Natural Image Detection Natural image manipulation detection aims to identify and localize local tamperingpredominantly splicing, copy-move, and object removalacross open-world scenes such as landscapes, urban environments, and complex crowd settings. Unlike facial forensics, which benefits from well-defined geometric topologies and strong structural priors, natural scene forensics must confront arbitrary semantic categories, highly diverse lighting conditions, non-uniform noise distributions, and complex post-processing degradations. Early Benchmarks on Physical and Statistical Traces. Pioneering efforts primarily focused on isolating specific physical or statistical inconsistencies introduced by manual editing. For instance, Columbia Hsu and Chang (2006) introduced rigorous testbed focusing on uncompressed image splicing to benchmark lighting inconsistencies. CASIA Dong et al. (2013) subsequently emerged as seminal benchmark that has anchored forensic research for over decade, providing standardized pixel-level ground-truth masks across diverse splicing and copy-move operations. Similarly, Coverage Wen et al. (2016) was specifically designed to evaluate copy-move tampering by pairing forged regions with genuine, geometrically similar objects, thereby challenging early keypointand block-based matching detectors. Scale Expansion and Semantic Realism. While foundational, early datasets often suffered from limited sample sizes, simplistic cut-and-paste artifacts, and constrained scene diversity. To overcome these limitations, subsequent benchmarks emphasized semantic harmony and dataset scale. DEFACTO-12k Mahfoudi et al. (2019) automated forgery synthesis by splicing semantically and geometrically compatible objects into background scenes. To bridge the gap between idealized laboratory data and in-the-wild manipulations, IMD2020 Novozamsky et al. (2020) curated real-world tampered images directly from the web, encompassing diverse compression qualities, social media filtering, and heterogeneous resolutions. Crucially, MIML Qu et al. (2024c) marked major milestone by constructing largescale benchmark featuring over 120,000 professionally edited forgeries paired with high-precision pixel-level annotations. By mitigating the critical scarcity of high-quality training data, MIML established an indispensable foundation for modern deep localization frameworks; its successor, MIMLv2 Qu et al. (2025b), further expanded dataset volume and fidelity through web-scale data collection and refined quality control. The Generative AI Paradigm Shift. Driven by the rapid proliferation of diffusion models and multimodal foundation models, the boundary of natural image manipulation has evolved from conventional cut-and-paste operations toward photorealistic local generative editing. Generative operations produce seamless boundaries, harmonious illuminations, and plausible textures, rendering traditional low-level boundary detectors largely ineffective. To keep pace with this generative evolution, CocoGlide Guillaro et al. (2023) and AutoSplice Jia et al. (2023) leverage text-guided diffusion models to automate local inpainting and object replacement, establishing new benchmarks for diffusion-based local forensics. Pushing this frontier further, So-Fake and its out-of-distribution counterpart So-Fake-OOD Huang et al. (2025b) comprehensively evaluate large-scale AI-edited forgeries across numerous state-of-the-art generative models, explicitly testing forensic generalizability and robustness in real-world social media contexts. ManipulationBench Jiang et al. (2026d) also comprises diverse high-quality image forgeries generated by updated AI-models such as Step1X-Edit Liu et al. (2025), Nano-Banana2 Nano-Banana2 Team (2026) and GPT-Image-2 GPT-Image-2 Team (2026). Collectively, this methodological progressionspanning from hand-crafted statistical benchmarks and massive manual datasets to modern generative editing suitesensures that vision forensic models can transcend facial-specific cues and generalize robustly across arbitrary, unconstrained natural scenes. 8.1.5 Face Anti-Spoofing Face anti-spoofing, also known as face presentation attack detection, aims to distinguish bona fide faces from physical presentation attacks such as printed photographs, video replays, and threedimensional masks. Compared with DeepFake detection, which targets digitally manipulated facial content, this subfield centers on spoofing media physically presented to the camera, and its datasets accordingly evolve along the axes of attack diversity, capture-device variety, and environmental realism. As one of the earliest dedicated benchmarks, CASIA-FASD Zhang et al. (2012) contains videos of 50 subjects with three representative attack types, namely warped printed photographs, printed photographs with cut-out eyes, and high-quality video replays, establishing standard early protocol for evaluating detectors against diverse two-dimensional attack media. Idiap ReplayAttack Chingovska et al. (2012) provides video clips of photo and video attack attempts against 50 clients, recorded under both controlled and adverse lighting conditions, and has served as the official testbed of the first two two-dimensional face anti-spoofing competitions, making it solid baseline for lighting-robust spoofing detection. To evaluate generalization under realistic mobile authentication scenarios, OULU-NPU Boulkenafet et al. (2017) collects videos of 55 subjects across three environments with six mobile devices of different resolutions, covering print and video-replay attacks together with standardized evaluation protocols that explicitly stress cross-device and crossenvironment robustness. MSU-MFSD Wen et al. (2015) complements this line with 280 bona fide 46 and attack recordings of 35 subjects captured by two mobile devices, incorporating three spoof attacks of printed photo, video replay, and mobile-device replay, and was originally designed to study spoofing cues through image distortion analysis. Advancing toward larger scale and richer modalities, CASIA-SURF Zhang et al. (2020a) scales up to 1,000 subjects and 21,000 videos with aligned RGB, depth, and infrared samples, providing comprehensive protocols that jointly examine multi-modal fusion and cross-method generalization. CelebA-Spoof Zhang et al. (2020b) further pushes the boundary of both scale and annotation richness, comprising 625,537 images of 10,177 subjects across 10 spoof types and 8 scenes, accompanied by 43 attributes covering face, illumination, environment, and spoof cues, thereby supporting attribute-aware and multi-task anti-spoofing learning. Moving from laboratory setups to unconstrained conditions, SiW (Spoofing in the Wild) Liu et al. (2018) offers 4,478 live and spoof videos of 165 subjects with 11 attack types spanning print, partial mask, replay, and makeup attacks, and defines multiple protocols to assess generalization toward unknown attacks. Finally, UniAttackData Yuan et al. (2024b) unifies physical and digital threats in single collection of 28,706 videos, where each of the 1,800 subjects undergoes two physical and twelve digital attacks launched by state-of-the-art deepfake and adversarial attack methods, providing the first large-scale benchmark for joint physical-digital face attack detection. Collectively, these datasets trace clear trajectory from controlled print/replay detection toward mobile, multi-modal, in-the-wild, and unified physical-digital evaluation, continuously driving anti-spoofing models toward attack-agnostic and device-agnostic generalization. 8.1.6 Document Anti-Spoofing Document anti-spoofing, commonly formulated as document presentation attack detection or recaptured document detection, targets distinct anti-forensic threat: an adversary first edits document in the digital domain and then re-presents it through printrescan or displayrecapture pipeline, such that the original tampering traces are concealed by the imaging process. Datasets in this subfield therefore emphasize diverse recapture channels, document templates, and capturing devices. DLC-2021 Polevoy et al. (2022), released for the Document Liveness Challenge, consists of video clips of synthetic identity documents from 10 mock document types captured in wide range of real-world conditions. It covers genuine laminated originals, unlaminated color copies, unlaminated grayscale copies, and screen recaptures recorded by two smartphones under varied illumination, occlusion, and projective distortion, providing practical benchmark for video-based document liveness verification. RSCID (Recaptured Student Card Image Dataset) Chen et al. (2022) focuses on practical recapturing attacks against student identity cards, organizing 12 card templates from five universities into five subsets collected with 11 imaging devices and 3 printing devices of markedly different quality, which enables domain-agnostic evaluation of document authentication across heterogeneous recapture pipelines. RDRD162 Chen et al. (2024c) substantially broadens the document diversity, comprising 5,346 samples built upon 162 document types such as patent certificates, graduation certificates, transcripts, and licenses, recaptured through 32 printerimager device combinations at high resolutions, and serving as standardized testbed for generalized recaptured document detection against unseen document contents. Extending the problem from still images to video, SCVD Chen et al. (2024b) is comprehensive student card video database containing more than 18,000 genuine, printer-captured, and screen-recaptured video frames collected under flashlight illumination, exploiting the distinctive reflections and temporal responses induced by active lighting to discriminate presentation attacks. For display-based attacks, ROD Chen et al. (2024d) mainly consists of black-and-white office documents and their screen-recaptured counterparts, targeting the color artifacts introduced by the screen-to-camera imaging chain and supporting robust detection of screen-recapture document images. SRDID162 Chen et al. (2025a) 47 further constructs screen-recaptured document image dataset with 162 templates, containing 162 genuine and 5,184 screen-recaptured samples, and is designed to evaluate detection methods that exploit moiré patterns and frequency-domain anomalies inherent to screen recapture. Collectively, these datasets chart the progression of document anti-spoofing from identity-document liveness videos to print recapture, and further to screen-recapture presentation attacks, providing increasingly realistic resources for exposing forgery traces concealed by re-imaging operations. 8.1.7 AI-Generated Video Detection With the explosive progress of text-to-video diffusion models and commercial video generation services, AI-generated video detection has emerged as pressing forensic problem, and its benchmarks have rapidly evolved from small collections of few open-source generators toward large-scale, multimodal, and scenario-aware evaluation suites. As the first million-scale benchmark in this domain, GenVideo Chen et al. (2026) collects millions of real and AI-generated videos, pairing millions of real videos with millions of generated videos synthesized by ten baseline generators, and further provides out-of-distribution testing with unseen generators together with systematic degradation robustness evaluation. LOKI Ye et al. (2025) pioneers comprehensive synthetic-data detection benchmark for large multimodal models, whose video part covers both open-source and commercial generators. Ivy-Fake Jiang et al. (2026a) is the first large-scale multimodal benchmark for explainable AIGC detection, offering tens of thousands of richly annotated training videos covering diverse generators. GVF Ma et al. (2025) constructs triplets of real video, text prompt, and generated videos from prompts synthesized by different open-source generators, and additionally probes detection against commercial generators, promoting temporally consistent forensic modeling. GVD Bai et al. (2024) assembles generated videos from diverse state-of-the-art generators across both text-to-video and image-to-video paradigms, providing realistic in-the-wild benchmark for cross-generator generalization. AIGCDBench Ma et al. (2026) pursues comprehensiveness and representativeness at new scale, covering tens of state-of-the-art generation models and hundreds of thousands of videos, and supporting extensive evaluations of dozens of detectors across heterogeneous scenarios. ComGenVid Zheng et al. (2025) targets the evaluation of training-free and zero-shot detectors, curating thousands of videos generated by recent high-fidelity commercial models against real videos under standardized short-clip protocol, thus stress-testing generalization to the latest closed-source generators. From the perspective of content plausibility, VideoPhy-2 Bansal et al. (2026) evaluates videos synthesized by seven state-of-the-art generators, annotated through human judgments of semantic adherence and physical commonsense, supplying action-centric videos with physical violations as challenging detection targets. MintVid Tan et al. (2026a) provides lightweight yet high-quality dataset of videos from many state-of-the-art generators, organized into general-content, facial, and fact-inconsistency parts, where the last part collects social-media videos whose factual errors can be objectively verified, supporting fact-based forensic reasoning. GenBuster-ID Wen et al. (2025a) and GenBuster-OOD Wen et al. (2025a) are derived from the 200K-scale GenBuster-200K Wen et al. (2025a) corpus, which pairs 100K real videos with 100K high-resolution videos synthesized by multiple generators; the former tests in-domain detection on seen generators under stricter generation settings, simulating the temporal arms race between generators and detectors. GenBuster++ Wen et al. (2026) extends the evaluation to cross-modal benchmark of 4,000 samples, containing 2,000 images and 2,000 video clips, each balanced between real and fake content generated by seven image and thirteen video generators, and subjected to twostage human filtering for reliable unified detection and explanation. Finally, RABench Liang et al. (2026) anchors evaluation on real-world crisis events, comprising 17,886 videos of 1,830 real anchor videos spanning ten social-risk categories and 16,056 generated clips from four open-source and five closed-source generators, jointly investigating detectability, human perception, and the reliability of detectors under social dissemination. Collectively, these benchmarks reflect the rapid co-evolution of video generation and forensic evaluation, shifting the research focus from generator-specific artifact fitting toward explainable, robust, and socially grounded detection of AI-generated videos. 8.1.8 Summary Overall, existing visual forensics datasets have significantly advanced detection and localization capabilities within their respective subfields. In biometric security, DeepFake benchmarks have expanded toward high-fidelity, in-the-wild facial manipulations, while face anti-spoofing has evolved from controlled print/replay attacks to multimodal, physical-digital benchmarks. In document forensics, datasets have progressed from basic identity liveness and text tampering to layout-consistent generative edits, realistic scanning noise, and screen-recapture presentation attacks. Concurrently, natural scene tampering benchmarks have shifted from classical splicing and copy-move operations to generative local editing. Furthermore, AI-generated image and video detection has surged from small, GAN-specific collections to million-scale suites encompassing diffusion foundation models, commercial video generators, multimodal explanations, and physical commonsense violations. Despite these individual advancements, the visual forensics landscape remains severely fragmented. Substantial discrepancies in data scale, real-to-fake ratios, supervision granularity (e.g., image-level labels vs. pixel-level masks), and evaluation protocols render these datasets insufficient for training unified visual forensics foundation models. While pioneer efforts like Omni-IML Qu et al. (2026b) and ForensicHub Du et al. (2026b) explored cross-domain benchmarking and highlighted task conflicts in multi-domain joint training, they remain constrained by standard academic data scales, limited sources, and restricted domain coverage. In contrast, DefakerOne2 establishes truly unified data foundation by systematically curating and harmonizing tens of millions of heterogeneous samples across AI-generated images/videos, DeepFakes, face and document anti-spoofing, and natural scene manipulations. Through systematic multi-version data composition experiments, DefakerOne2 rigorously analyzes the cross-domain complementarity, transferability, and gradient interference among diverse forensic artifacts, paving the way for principled data mixtures and robust foundation models for full-spectrum visual forensics. 8.2 Methods Vision forensic methodologies have progressively evolved from task-specific vision models toward multimodal large language models (MLLMs) Team et al. (2026). Early approaches predominantly developed dedicated architectures tailored to specific tampering scenariossuch as text-region locators for document forgery, pixel-level segmentation networks for natural image tampering, facial classifiers for DeepFake detection, and synthetic artifact detectors for AI-generated media. Although these specialized models have achieved remarkable success within their respective niches, their underlying architectures, input-output paradigms, and assumed artifact priors remain inherently fragmented. Recently, MLLMs have garnered significant interest in fake image detection and interpretation, owing to their advanced visual-semantic comprehension, interactive natural-language reasoning, and unified interface representations. Consequently, this section first categorizes traditional unimodal vision methods across standard forensic subdomains, subsequently reviews recent MLLM-based explorations in unified detection, localization, and reasoning, and finally discusses the remaining gaps toward building unified vision forensics foundation model. 8.2.1 Vision Forensic Models Historically, visual media forensics has been explored through isolated subfieldsprimarily DeepFake detection, AI-generated content (AIGC) identification, document tampering localization, natural image manipulation detection, and anti-spoofing. These domains diverge considerably in their targets and operational contexts: DeepFake detection concentrates on facial manipulations such as identity swapping and expression reenactment; AI-generated detection targets fully synthesized images or video sequences; document forensics focuses on low-visibility text alterations in receipts, contracts, and scene-text images; and natural image manipulation localization addresses local editing operations like splicing, copy-move, and inpainting. As result, early methods were developed independently rather than under unified framework, relying on domain-specific artifact priors, distinct output formats, and disjoint evaluation benchmarks. In the DeepFake Detection domain Hopf et al. (2026), tasks are conventionally framed as binary classification problems targeting facial identity, texture, frequency, or blending inconsistencies. Capsule-Net Nguyen et al. (2019) pioneered the use of capsule networks to model spatial arrangements among local facial components via dynamic routing. RECCE Cao et al. (2022) exploits reconstruction discrepancies between pristine and manipulated faces within reconstruction-classification framework. SPSL Liu et al. (2021a) captures phase-spectrum anomalies and high-frequency upsampling artifacts via shallow spectral features. To improve cross-generator generalization, SBI Shiohara and Yamasaki (2022) generates self-blended images from single pristine faces to reproduce common blending boundaries and statistical inconsistencies. Sia Sun et al. (2022) introduces an informationtheoretic self-information attention mechanism to guide network focus toward discriminative forged regions and channels. CDFA Lin et al. (2024) proposes curricular dynamic forgery augmentations to progressively synthesize challenging samples, while DINOMAC Qu et al. (2026a) applies LoRAbased adapter tuning Hu et al. (2022) to DINOv3 Siméoni et al. (2025) alongside Multi-Aspect Classification head to minimize overlooked subtle cues, achieving state-of-the-art robustness. In the AI-Generated Image Detection domain Gushchin et al. (2026), efforts primarily center on distinguishing authentic imagery from outputs synthesized by GANs, diffusion models, or autoregressive generators. UnivFD Ojha et al. (2023) leverages the transferable feature representations of vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) to achieve open-world fake image detection with lightweight linear probe. FatFormer Liu et al. (2024) introduces forgery-aware adaptive Transformer to dynamically capture generative fingerprints across varied model families. Forensic-MOE Fang et al. (2025) incorporates Mixture-of-Experts architecture to mine complementary forensic traces. CO-SPY Cheng et al. (2025) couples semantic features with pixel-level artifact representations for multi-cue synthetic image discrimination, while Effort Yan et al. (2024a) explicitly decouples content-related and forgery-related representations via orthogonal subspace decomposition to mitigate overfitting. Complementarily, DRCT Chen et al. (2024a) exploits diffusion reconstruction contrastive training to achieve universal detection of diffusion-synthesized images. In the Document Tampering Detection and Localization domain Wong et al. (2025), the objective is to precisely identify subtle, fine-grained text alterations. DTD Qu et al. (2023) tackles lowcontrast visual discrepancies by introducing Frequency Perception Head and Multi-view Iterative Decoder that integrate JPEG compression artifacts with multi-view representations. FFDN Chen et al. (2024h) decomposes and fuses spatial and frequency cues using visual and wavelet-like enhancement modules to capture delicate compression and boundary irregularities. CAFTB Song et al. (2025) employs dual-branch architecture that models spatial and noise domains concurrently via cross-attention. TIFDM Dong et al. (2024) couples multi-domain trace enhancement with multiscale context aggregation for precise text manipulation localization. Additionally, DS-Net Qu et al. (2026d) achieves robust cross-generator generalization by pretraining on generic natural images while synergizing image-level classification with pixel-level localization. In the Natural Image Manipulation Detection and Localization domain Ma et al. (2024), networks are typically designed to jointly output image-level authenticity decisions and pixel-level tampering masks. MVSS-Net Dong et al. (2022) enforces multi-view, multi-scale supervision using boundary artifacts and noise residuals. CAT-Net Kwon et al. (2022) leverages DCT-domain representations to model subtle JPEG compression discrepancies. APSC-Net Qu et al. (2025b) introduces adaptive feature fusion to capture multi-scale tampering clues, whereas IML-ViT Ma et al. (2023) adopts Vision Transformers to capture long-range non-semantic inconsistencies across disparate image patches. TruFor Guillaro et al. (2023) fuses RGB features with learned noise fingerprints, treating tampered regions as anomalies relative to background consistency. Mesorch Zhu et al. (2025a) deploys hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture to characterize manipulated areas at mesoscopic level. Omni-IML Qu et al. (2026b) represents an early effort toward cross-domain unified forensics using modality-adaptive encoder and dynamic-weight decoder. Finally, RITA Zhu et al. (2025b) resolves dimensional collapse in composite tamperings by formulating sequential edits as an ordered process, and Web-IML Qu et al. (2025b) refines accuracy via error-feedback learning mechanisms. In the Face Anti-Spoofing domain Yu et al. (2024), the goal is to distinguish bonafide faces from presentation attacks such as printed photos, replayed videos, and 3D masks, and more recently from digitally manipulated faces. Because privacy regulations often forbid reusing the source data of deployed model, SDA-FAS Liu et al. (2022b) performs source-free adaptation by pairing contrastive domain alignment module that treats the frozen source model as prototypes with self-supervised patch-shuffle exploration. MD-FAS Yu et al. (2025) instead formalizes model updating, where pre-trained detector must absorb new domain without catastrophic forgetting. To escape handcrafted artifact priors, FLIP Srivatsan et al. (2023) grounds visual representations in natural language by aligning image features with an ensemble of class descriptions derived from CLIP Radford et al. (2021) text encoders, and further applies multimodal contrastive learning so that zero-shot transfer surpasses five-shot adaptive ViTs. Addressing the coexistence of physical and digital attacks, micro-disturbance detection Yu et al. (2024) relabels subtly perturbed faces (color jitter, screen simulation, JPEG compression, Gaussian blur) as forgeries and adopts two-stage masked-image-modeling pre-training followed by linear fine-tuning. MVP-FAS Yu et al. (2025) is vision-language face anti-spoofing method that addresses drawbacks of existing CLIP-based prompt learning via multi-view slot attention and multi-text patch alignment, leveraging paraphrased text prompts to enhance cross-domain generalization for face anti-spoofing. Finally, MoAE-CR Chen et al. (2025c) deploys fine-grained mixture of attack experts on CLIP features with distance rule prioritizing outlier-like features, plus disentanglement and cluster-distillation regularization to enlarge inter-class margins. In the Document Anti-Spoofing domain Tapia et al. (2026), the question is whether submitted identity or office document was genuinely captured or re-presented through printing, displaying, and re-photographing. Since curating real attack instruments is expensive and privacy-sensitive, synthetic ID card generation Benalcazar et al. (2023) explores computer-vision-based and GAN-based synthesis to augment fraud-detection training, preserving print-attack accuracy while incurring only marginal drop on screen-capture attacks. Open-set ID card detection Markham et al. (2024) pushes this toward unseen attack instruments by translating genuine cards with four GAN-based image translation models in neural style transfer manner, so that synthetic presentations complement real ones. Against practical recapturing, domain-agnostic authentication Chen et al. (2022) mimics 51 the forensic inspection procedure by feeding questioned document and reference sample into Siamese network trained with forensic similarity function under triplet and normalized softmax losses, generalizing across devices, substrates, recapturing channels, and document types. Because moiré interference is entangled with legitimate printing texture, moiré-texture disentanglement Li et al. (2025b) explicitly separates chromatic and moiré artifacts from natural document texture for display-recapture detection. CMA-Doc Chen et al. (2024d) derives pixel-level distortion model of screen-recaptured documents and injects the resulting chromaticity map into transformer backbone as multi-modal prompt tokens, remaining effective after social-network compression and downscaling. Complementarily, moiré spectral augmentation with masked frequency modeling Chen et al. (2025a) enhances the spectral components attributable to moiré distortion (FMAG) and adopts masked frequency reconstruction to learn transferable spectral representations. In the AI-Generated Video Detection domain Chen et al. (2026), detectors must additionally reason over temporal coherence while generators evolve faster than labeled data accumulates. Spatiotemporal anomaly learning Bai et al. (2024) trains two ResNet sub-detectors on RGB frames and RAFT optical flow respectively and fuses their frame-level decisions. DeCoF Ma et al. (2025) shows through probing that spatial-artifact detectors generalize poorly, and therefore learns frame consistency by suppressing spatial cues during feature extraction, accompanied by an open dataset spanning commercial models such as Sora and Veo. Pursuing label-free deployment, D3 Zheng et al. (2025) grounds detection in Newtonian second-order dynamics, computing difference-ofdifferences features from consecutive frames and separating real from generated videos by their distributional divergence without any training. ReStraV Internò et al. (2025) exploits the perceptual straightening property that natural motion traces straighter trajectories in representation space, encoding frames with frozen encoder and classifying 21-dimensional descriptor of stepwise distances and turning angles. DeMamba Chen et al. (2026) contributes plug-and-play Detail Mamba module that propagates discriminative low-level details across frames with linear-complexity longrange modeling. Likewise training-free, SPLIT Hyun and Kim (2026) scores two-step temporal roughness together with local spatial motion incoherence over patch tokens of frozen encoder, multiplicatively fusing them so as to sustain high fake recall at an ultra-low false-positive rate on fully generated and partially edited videos Lin et al. (2025). Overall, while domain-specific vision models have achieved remarkable milestones, most remain constrained by narrow task definitions, relying heavily on specialized data formats, handcrafted artifact priors, and isolated output representations.

sections.title: 8.2.2 MLLMs for FIDL
sections.content: By producing natural language outputs, MLLMs deliver human-readable interpretability by construction, which constitutes distinct advantage over conventional vision-only models when they are deployed as AIGC or tampered-image detectors. Subsequent research has largely revolved around balancing detection accuracy, reasoning depth, and inference latency. TextSleuth Qu et al. (2024a) attains interpretable detection by incorporating dedicated perception head. Omni-IML Qu et al. (2026b) mitigates hallucination through decoupled design, whereas TextShield-R1 Qu et al. (2026c) further improves generalization via cross-domain pre-training, text-specific reinforcement learning, and OCR-based rectification. X2-DFD Chen et al. (2024f) proposes an explainable and extensible MLLM-based framework for DeepFake detection. Ivy-xDetector Jiang et al. (2026a) adopts chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm that generates an explanation before issuing the final verdict, at the cost of emitting massive number of tokens. 52 To relieve this latency bottleneck, FakeVLM Wen et al. (2025b) proposes classify-then-explain pipeline; although it resolves the efficiency issue, its textual explanations remain vague and nonspecific, and extensive experiments further reveal its fragility on certain tampered images. Tackling the computational overhead of CoT from complementary angle, Fake-HR1 Jiang et al. (2026b) designs hybrid reasoning chain tailored to reduce this burden in FID scenarios. FakeShield Xu et al. (2025) integrates segmentation module into the MLLM, marrying the interpretability of language reasoning with the pixel-level precision of segmentation networks. Veritas Tan et al. (2026b) introduces an R1-like multi-stage training procedure to strengthen forgery interpretability. Extending this line to the video domain, BusterX Wen et al. (2025a) recasts AI-generated video detection as visual reasoning task in which the generated reasoning chain itself serves as the detector. BusterX++ Wen et al. (2026) further unifies image and video forensics within single cross-modal MLLM, demonstrating that one-stage pure reinforcement learning driven by sparse outcome rewards matches or surpasses the conventional supervised-fine-tuning-then-reinforcementlearning pipeline while eliciting spontaneous cross-modal capability transfer. Skyra Li et al. (2026b) grounds its verdicts in human-perceivable artifacts by explicitly localizing spatio-temporal anomalies, and is trained through supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO-based reinforcement learning with asymmetric rewards. VideoVeritas Tan et al. (2026a) couples joint preference alignment with perception pretext reinforcement learning, which optimizes general spatio-temporal grounding and self-supervised object counting as pretext tasks rather than the detection objective directly. 8.2.3 Summary In summary, vision forensic methods have evolved from domain-specific detectors toward MLLMdriven explainable frameworks, yet strong foundation-model baseline for full-domain vision forensics remains absent. Conventional models are typically tailored to single subdomain, relying on domain-specific artifacts, specialized architectures, and fixed output formats; consequently, they struggle with cross-domain forgery distributions and cannot accommodate the coupled requirements of detection and localization. Recent MLLM-based methods instead offer unified interface, joint visual-semantic understanding, and natural-language explanation, but their optimization objective often drifts toward reasoning-chain generation or descriptive interpretation rather than the core forensic goals of authenticity verification and forgery localization. As result, they fail to fully exploit large-scale image-level labels and pixel-level masks, and are therefore ill-suited to serve as stable full-domain forensic baselines. Efforts toward unification do exist but remain incomplete: Omni-IML Qu et al. (2026b) and ForensicHub Du et al. (2026b) expose the promise and the challenges of unified forensics from the modeling and evaluation-protocol perspectives, whereas DefakerOne Team (2026) scales training to millions of digitally forged samples yet still covers substantially narrower forensic scope. To close this gap, DefakerOne2 is built upon Qwen3.5 Qwen3.5 Team (2026) + DINOMAC Qu et al. (2026a) backbone and, supported by multi-domain data composition experiments, systematically investigates how heterogeneous forensic data can be converted into unified detection, localization, and generalization capabilities. In doing so, it markedly broadens forensic coverage relative to DefakerOne Team (2026) and establishes direct, strong baseline for full-domain vision forensics foundation models.

sections.title: 10 Limitations
sections.content: DefakerOne2 is first attempt at training single unified model for broader vision-forensics coverage. As with all deep modelsand indeed with human examinersit is not perfect and can still fail, even on samples whose anomalies are obvious to the human eye. Such failures can be reduced by incorporating more targeted training data that shares similar characteristics with the cases in question. In addition, to mitigate white-box attacks against our deployed online model, only small subset of outdated in-house data is used for training. DefakerOne2 is therefore intended as vision foundation that attains stronger generalization on downstream forensic tasks with less task-specific training dataa starting point, rather than finished model that performs perfectly in every case. Owing to limited computational resources, the segmentation module is trained exclusively on regionally tampered samples; neither authentic nor fully-generated samples are included. Consequently, the segmentation prediction may be inconsistent with the classification prediction. In such cases, the classification prediction should take precedence: the predicted mask is designed only to highlight cues in images that are already suspected of being forged.

sections.title: 11 Domestic GPU/Accelerator Adaptation
sections.content: For informal exploratory experiments, domestically manufactured computing GPUs were utilized. In supported business scenarios, we have completed the training migration and deep adaptation of the Qwen3.5 series models onto the Huawei Ascend platform, enabling the full end-to-end pipeline including model loading, data processing, forward computation, backward propagation, parameter updates, and checkpoint recovery. To address differences across computing platforms in operator implementation, data types, and numerical precision, we established layered precision alignment mechanism ranging from critical operators to full-network training. By systematically comparing intermediate tensors, output logits, gradients, loss curves, and downstream task performance, we ensured that the migrated models maintain training convergence and business accuracy consistent with the baseline environment. At present, for the full Qwen3.5 series of both dense and MoE models, we support up to 256K longcontext training for both pure-text training and vision-language multimodal training. In this business scenario, under the same training configuration, Huawei Ascend accelerators (A3) deliver an average 11% improvement in single-step training performance compared with the original baseline (the Pingtouge series), and an end-to-end training speed improvement of approximately 12%13%. In long-duration test over 20 epochs, the overall training time was reduced by 13.4%.
